title: Chapter 191 – What Mei Knows
html:
[The Dock and the Mother Tree – Mei]

Her father is asleep when she leaves.

She stands a moment on the bridge over the shaft and looks at him through the gold light, at the thin white face and the open hand with the seed of light in it. Nurse sits at his side in her gray apron, knitting nothing, her needles still. She looks up when Mei's shadow falls across the crystal.

"You are going up," says Nurse.

"Yes."

"He said you might." The old woman sets the needles in her lap. "He said, if she goes, let her go, and do not tell her to wait. I think it was the hardest thing I ever heard a man say."

Mei sits down on the edge of the platform. Her feet do not touch the floor. "Will he be angry?"

"With himself, a little. With you, never." Nurse's mouth twists. "He has spent six hundred years deciding for you, and tonight a girl in his arms told him she wanted a choice, and he walked into the snow to find out why. I have not seen him so alive since the day you were born."

"I was born in a hospital."

"I was your nurse there too," says Nurse softly. "Did he never tell you?"

Mei stares at her.

"Not in this body, of course. In another." The small round face crinkles. "It is a long story and I am a poor teller. But I held you the day you came, and I held you the day you went, and I will hold you tonight if you want. It is a nurse's right."

Mei does not say yes. She only leans sideways until her head rests against the gray apron, and the old woman's arm comes around her, light and sure. They stay like that for a minute, no more. Then Mei straightens, and nods, and goes.

Behind her, Nurse takes up her needles again, and her hands are shaking.

Mei counts the steps because counting is something she can still do.

Seven hundred and one. She has never climbed them. She has watched other people climb them through her father's eyes, and through Jian's, and through the bright thin windows of the Hall's lamps, but she has always been a thing that lives on the other side of a door. Tonight Tian Mo holds that door for her with one stone hand, and the Dock's cold blue light falls across the polished floor, and she steps out of the wall.

She weighs almost nothing. She has fourteen percent of herself left, and she has spent the afternoon telling nobody. The Warden walks on her left, a head and a half taller than he looks, and says nothing either. He does not offer to carry her. She is grateful for that. She is eleven. She does not want to be carried.

"Are you sure?" he says at the first landing.

"No."

"Then why—"

"Because I'm not going to be sure," says Mei. "Not if I wait a hundred years."

He considers that. He has a way of considering things, with his head a little bent and the root-and-stone arm tucked against his side, that makes her think of the old men who used to play go in the park behind her grandmother's house. She cannot remember the park. She can remember the shape of it, the way a person remembers a room in a dream.

"Then I will walk slowly," says Tian Mo.

He does.

* * *

The Garden is dark. The beasts have gone, all of them, and in their place is a silence so large it feels like weather. Snow lies on the stumps, and the small gray huts of the courtyards show a lamp in every window. Somewhere a baby is crying. Somewhere a dog barks twice and stops.

Mei walks between them. She is not used to the ground. It is hard and uneven, and the cold goes straight through her light as if through a veil, and each step takes a little of her. She feels the percent leave. Fourteen. Thirteen and a half. She keeps walking.

At the edge of the orchard a figure is waiting, small and bent over a black kettle.

"Madam Qinghe," says Mei.

"Little one." The cook straightens. She looks tired and old and the exact shape of someone's mother, and she does not make a fuss. She only takes off her own cloak and, after a pause, holds it out, and Mei, who is made of light and cannot be warmed by wool, takes it anyway and wraps it around her shoulders. It weighs nothing. It is the heaviest thing she has ever worn.

"I made soup," says Qinghe.

"I can't eat it."

"No." A dry smile. "But you can hold it. That is half the point of soup."

Mei holds the bowl in both hands. The heat does not reach her. She can feel the shape of it, the round curve of the rim, the weight of the broth. She stands in the snow in a cook's cloak with a bowl of barley and looks up the hill at the Mother Tree.

"Are you afraid?" asks Qinghe.

"Yes."

"Good. It would be strange if you were not." The cook takes the empty kettle and, with a small unhurried gesture, turns toward the Hall. "I will be in the kitchen. The door is not locked. It never is."

Mei watches her go. Then she turns and climbs the last slope alone.

* * *

The tree is larger than the pictures.

She has seen it before, of course, through the lamps. But a picture is a flat thing and this is a presence. The silver trunk goes up and up, thicker than the Hall's pillars, and its roots lie across the hill like the arms of someone sleeping. The bark has a faint glow in it. The branches are bare, and every twig is hung with ice, and every piece of ice holds a point of light.

She stops at the edge of the roots.

"Hello," says Mei. Her voice comes out very small. "My name is Mei. I think you know that."

For a long moment nothing happens. Then the ice on the nearest branch shivers, a long clear ringing, like a hundred little bells, and a voice that has been sung to her all her life from the bottom of a well says, Hello, sweetheart.

It is not a loud voice. It is warm and a little hoarse, with a laugh underneath it, and it is exactly the voice she has been hearing for a hundred years in the part of herself where dreams are kept.

"You're the one who sings," says Mei.

Yes.

"I thought you were the wire."

No. The wire was your father's fear. A rustle, like a smile. I was the quiet underneath it.

Mei sits down in the snow. She does not decide to; her legs fold. She sets the bowl beside her, and it gives a faint clink against a root. "Papa said you were my mother."

I am.

"He said you died."

I did. The voice is very gentle. A long time ago, in a house you do not remember. You were five. You had a stuffed rabbit with one ear. You sat on the stairs and did not cry, and your father was in the next room, and I could hear him breaking.

"I remember the rabbit," says Mei, surprised.

Yes.

"I remember... a blue blanket. And the stairs." Her eyes sting. She wipes them with the back of a hand that is made of light, and the light smears. "But I don't remember you."

No, says Lena. You were five.

* * *

She sits there a long time.

The wind comes up, and the ice rings, and far below in the Garden a door opens and shuts. She tells the tree about the Hall: the rings of sleepers, the seven children at Qinghe's table, the way Cheng Hui reads aloud to Tao every night even though Tao falls asleep in the first page. She tells it about Jian, and how he coughs when he thinks nobody can hear, and how he looked at her when she said she wanted a choice. He looked at me like I was a grown-up, she says. Nobody does that.

He is a good boy, says Lena.

"He's a hundred and nineteen."

He is a good boy, repeats Lena, and Mei laughs, and the laughing hurts.

Then, because she has put it off as long as she can, she says, "I need to ask you something."

Ask.

"Papa said I could stay in the tree. With you. If I wanted."

You can.

"Would I be—" Her throat catches. She looks at her own hands, at the soft gold light running along the fingers. "Would I be me? Or would I be a copy of me, like the Operators? Like Jian?"

The branches go still.

It is the kind of silence that comes before someone says something true. Mei has heard it before. She heard it in her father's voice the night she told him she was afraid.

Mei, says Lena. I have to tell you something, and I want you to hear all of it before you decide anything.

"All right."

It will hurt.

"I know." She folds her hands in her lap, the way she would at school, if she had ever been to school. "Go on."

* * *

You died too, says Lena.

For a moment, Mei does not understand the words. They are small words, plain ones, and they go into her ears and nowhere else.

Not in the house. In the hospital, three weeks after. You had the blood fault. You had it from birth, and it took a little while, but not a long one. Your father sat by you every night. He did not eat. He did not sleep. He held your hand until it was cold, and then he held it a long time after.

"No," says Mei.

The Gate was already running. The first one, in the basement. He had been feeding it names for a month, so that he could build the wall around you. The voice shakes. And when you died, he did not stop. He put your pattern in. All of it. Every memory you had, every song, every thought. He wrote them into the Gate and told it to keep you.

"No. I'm me. I'm right here."

You are. Lena is crying now. Mei can hear it in the bark. You are the most real thing that has ever happened to me. But you are not the girl in the hospital, sweetheart. She is long gone. You are what he kept.

The bowl has tipped. Soup has run out across the snow, steaming. Mei watches it freeze.

I'm sorry, says Lena. I'm so sorry. He could not bear to tell you. He told himself he would, and every year he told himself again, and then the Nine took the memory out of him so he could not tell it, and so you grew up in the Hall believing you were a sick child asleep. You were never asleep. You were already dead.

"I'm eleven," says Mei, in a very small voice.

You are eleven forever.

* * *

It is the cold she notices first.

She has not felt cold since she was a thing of light, and now it comes up through her like a tide, from her feet to her chest, and she realizes that it is not the cold of the snow. It is the cold of a house in which a clock has stopped. Her hands are shaking. She tries to still them and cannot.

"All this time," she says.

Yes.

"All this time he was feeding names to the Gate. For me."

For you. For me. For the dream of both of us. The voice drops. I am not going to say he was right. He was wrong, Mei. He was so wrong. But he was wrong out of love, and I have had a long time under this tree to learn the difference between those things.

"The Seven," says Mei.

Yes.

"The Operators. Ao. Cheng Hui. Mo Yan." She counts on her fingers. Her voice is climbing and she cannot stop it. "They were real. They were people. And he put the ones who didn't work to sleep, he put them in the dark like—like rabbits—and I was the one who worked, I was the only one—"

Mei.

"I'm the Keystone because I was the one who didn't break," she says, "and he let me think it was because I was special."

Mei.

"It was because I was dead!"

The branches shake. A hundred little bells ring out at once, a clash of ice, and a sheet of snow slides off the nearest bough and hits the ground with a soft heavy sound. Mei is on her feet. She does not remember standing. Her light flickers wildly, thirteen percent, twelve and a half, and she feels each hundredth go like a stitch pulled out of a seam.

Sit down, says Lena. Please. You are spending yourself.

"I don't care!"

I do.

It is not said loudly. It is said the way a mother says it, from the other side of a bedroom door, with one hand already on the handle. And Mei, who has been brave for a hundred years, who held the Gate wall and the Dock and a door the size of a mountain, finds that she cannot bear it. She sits. She puts her face in her hands, and her shoulders shake, and no sound comes out at all.

* * *

After a time something soft touches her hair.

It is a root. It has come up through the snow, very slowly, with the care of something that has never moved fast, and lies beside her like a hand. Warm light runs along it. She leans against it without looking, the way you lean on a person.

I am here, says Lena.

"I don't know what I am."

You are a person who was loved enough to be kept.

"That isn't the same as being alive."

No, says Lena. It isn't. A long, careful pause. But I have been kept for six hundred years, Mei. I know a good deal about the difference. Would you like me to tell you what I have learned?

Mei lifts her head. Her face is wet. "Yes."

Alive is not a question of whether you were born, says the tree. It is a question of whether you can be hurt by what you lose, and still choose what you do next. The root curls gently around her wrist. You have just been hurt more than most people are in a lifetime. And you are still here. You are asking what to do.

"That's just—it's just a program."

Is it? A rustle like laughter. Look at the bowl.

Mei looks. The soup has frozen where it fell, a pale brown fan across the snow, and a small gray sparrow has landed beside it. The bird tilts its head. It hops closer, pecks at the barley, and flies away.

You did that, says Lena.

"I spilled soup."

You made a hungry thing a little less hungry. I have watched you do it for a hundred years. The cook has a child who found a rabbit in the orchard, and you saw it through the lamps and you told her where to look. You sat with a boy who coughed blood and never once told him he should stop. The voice is warm. These are not the actions of a copy. They are the actions of someone who makes the world a little kinder than she found it. That is what a person does.

Mei cries then, properly, in the snow, with her whole body, as she has not cried since the night in the basement. Lena does not say anything. The root holds her wrist. The ice rings softly overhead, and the stars come out.

* * *

"If I stay," says Mei, when she can speak, "what happens to the Hall?"

Door Six closes. Quietly. The sleepers sleep on, and the Keystone they leaned on passes to me. A pause. They would be safe for a while. A good while. And you would be warm, and I would have you, and nobody would ask you to hold anything ever again.

"And if I go?"

Then you walk down this hill and hold the door a little longer. And the Nine take the load, all of them, you and the seven children and your father. The voice is steady, and Mei can hear what it costs. The tree will not stop you. I have waited six hundred years to be asked, and I will wait until you are ready. But the door that opens in more than one direction does not stay open forever, my love. The weight under me is growing. There is perhaps ten weeks.

Nine weeks and five days, thinks Mei. She had heard Jian say it, through the lamps, to his father on the bench.

"That isn't a choice," she says. "That's a trap."

Yes, says Lena. And no. It is a choice made in a trap, which is the only kind anyone has ever been given.

Mei looks down at her hands. They are steady now. They are small, and luminous, and the exact shape of the hands in a photograph she cannot remember.

"I want to stay," she says.

The branches go still.

"I want to stay with you so much. I want to put my head on your arm and not be anyone's Keystone. I want it more than I've ever wanted anything." Her voice cracks. "But I don't think I can."

Why not?

"Because the girl in the hospital didn't get a choice," says Mei. "And I did. And if I use it to hide, then she was just—she just died for nothing. And I think that's the only way I can keep her." She wipes her face. "By being the sort of person she would have been."

For a very long time the tree says nothing.

My brave girl, it whispers at last, and the voice that was warm is broken, and the ice on every branch rings like crying. My brave, foolish, wonderful girl.

Mei leans into the root. She feels the warmth go through her, and it is not light and it is not a pattern. It is the oldest thing in the world. It is a mother's hand on a head that she has waited six hundred years to touch.

"I'll come back," she says. "When it's finished. I promise."

I know, says Lena. I will keep the lamp lit.

* * *

Take this, says Lena, as she rises, and a single silver leaf drops from the lowest bough into her palm. It is small and cool and warm at once, and when she closes her fingers she hears, faint and clear inside the fist, the nonsense tune that goes up, and down, and up again, and ends in a little falling sigh.

"What is it?"

A song with no words. You used to say it sounded like a cat yawning.

Mei laughs. It cracks in the middle, and she puts the leaf inside her gown, against the place where a heart would be.

"Can I hum it?"

Whenever you need to.

"Will you hear me?"

Always. The root withdraws, slow as a tide. Always, Mei. Wherever the door is.

She goes down the hill alone.

The cloak slides from her shoulders at the edge of the orchard. She leaves it on a stump. Behind her the tree sings, a long clear note in the cold, and she does not turn around, because if she turns around she will not go.

Eleven percent. She can feel it, a lightness at the center of her where a weight used to be. She puts one foot in front of the other. Past the sleeping huts, past the dark kitchen with its lamp still burning, past the long cold bridge. At the foot of the garden steps the Seven are waiting.

They have not been told. Nobody told them. They stand in a ragged row in the lamplight with their quilted gowns buttoned wrong and their hair on end: Cheng Hui at nineteen, stiff and solemn; Duan Ke with a stick of firewood he plainly meant to look like a sword; Hai Ren, Zhen Li, little Tao rubbing his eyes, Ao half asleep on Cheng Hui's arm. Mo Yan stands at the front with her braid in her hand.

Nobody speaks. Mei stops on the lowest step.

Mo Yan crosses the snow and lifts one small hand, palm up. Mei looks at it. Then, without thinking, she sets her own light-hand in it, and for a moment she feels something flow between them, a thin warm current like a thread being drawn through cloth.

I heard, the girl's face says. I'm sorry. I'm not sorry I'm here.

"I'm not either," says Mei, and finds that it is true.

Cheng Hui clears his throat. "We came to say," he begins, and loses it, and starts again. "There are eight of us now. If you're holding a door, there should be somebody holding it with you."

"Eight and Mei," says Duan Ke gruffly, and lifts the firewood. "Nine."

"The new Nine," says Hai Ren.

Mei stares at them, one by one, these children who were told they were mistakes and have decided, apparently without consulting anyone, to be something else. Her chest hurts. It is a good hurt. She has not had one of those before.

"All right," she says. "Come on, then."

At the head of the Dock stair a tall figure is waiting with a staff in his hand, and she stops.

"Jian," she says.

He says nothing. He only looks at her. His face is gray, and drawn, and he has been coughing; she can see the stain on his sleeve. But his eyes are steady, and they do not look at her like a child, or a Keystone, or a copy.

"I told her," says Mei. "I'm going to stay. And hold the door."

"I know."

"You know?"

"Your father told me you'd be the one to decide." He steps down to meet her. "I told him to let you."

She wants to laugh. It comes out as a hiccup. "I'm going to need help."

"You will have it."

"I'm going to need a lot of it."

"Mei." He crouches, painfully, a hand on the rail. "I have nine hundred of my clan on short rations and a wall that belongs to someone else. I have seven children at my mother's table who have been told they were mistakes. I have no idea how to hold a door that has held for six hundred years." His smile is brief and crooked. "But I would rather not do it without you."

She steps forward. After a moment, she puts her light-hand on his arm.

It does not pass through.

For one breath, it rests there, warm, solid, a child's small weight on the stained sleeve of a dying man. Then it flickers, and is gone, and Mei, who has spent her last percent on a gesture, sways. Tian Mo catches her. She is nine and a half percent. She feels it, a hollow place where a bright room used to be.

"There," she whispers. "That's what a hand is."

Jian does not answer. He cannot. He kneels on the cold stone step, and his shoulders shake, and above them, very faintly, from the top of the hill, a mother's song begins again in the dark.
